steps: Build an array and print its dtype.
Call `astype(int)` and print the new array.
Print the original array to show it did not change.
Converting with astype.visual:
a = [1.7, 2.9]  dtype float64
astype(int)   → [1 2] dtype int64
original a    → [1.7 2.9] (untouched)
Converting with astype.realWorld: A model expects integer class ids but the labels arrived as floats after a merge; `astype(int)` is the explicit conversion at that boundary.
mistakes: Assuming `astype` edits the array in place — it returns a new one.
Casting to int to "round" values, when it truncates.
Repeated casts in a hot loop instead of casting once at load time.
revision: astype returns a new array with the requested dtype.
Convert once at the boundary, not inside the loop.

steps: Create `np.array([250], dtype=np.uint8)`.
Add 10 and print the result.
Check the value against `np.iinfo(np.uint8).max`.
Overflow is silent.visual:
uint8 range: 0 … 255
250 + 10 = 260 → 260 − 256 = 4
no warning, no exception
Overflow is silent.realWorld: Sensor counters and image pixel arithmetic are the classic overflow sites: a brightness increase wraps 250 → 4 and the image goes dark instead of clipping.
mistakes: Expecting NumPy to raise on overflow like a Python int.
Choosing uint8 for counters that can pass 255.
Adding arrays of different integer widths and assuming the wider one wins.
revision: Integer overflow wraps silently.
Check `np.iinfo(dtype).max` against the real range, or promote.

steps: Create the same values as float32 and as float64.
Print `dtype` and `nbytes` for both.
Compare the total bytes for one million elements.
Smaller dtype, smaller memory.visual:
float64 → 8 bytes/value
float32 → 4 bytes/value
1,000,000 values: 8 MB vs 4 MB
Smaller dtype, smaller memory.realWorld: A feature matrix that fits in RAM as float32 but not as float64 is the difference between training locally and needing a bigger machine.
mistakes: Downcasting float64 data without checking the precision loss.
Assuming float32 speeds up every operation — some libraries upcast internally.
Forgetting that `nbytes` counts the buffer, not the Python object overhead.
revision: `itemsize` is bytes per element; `nbytes` is the whole buffer.
float32 halves memory at the cost of precision.

astype truncates toward zero.syntax: a.astype(np.int64)  # drops the fraction, does not round
steps: Create `[1.9, -1.9]` and cast to int.
Print the result and note both values moved toward zero.
Compare with `np.round(a).astype(int)`.
astype truncates toward zero.realWorld: Prices stored as floats and cast to integer cents lose a cent per item; the honest fix is rounding first or storing cents as integers from the start.
mistakes: Using `astype(int)` as a rounding step.
Assuming negative numbers round down; they truncate up toward zero.
Casting before summing instead of after.
revision: Cast truncates toward zero.
Round first when the fraction matters.

steps: Create a string array from two numeric strings.
Cast it to float and print the dtype.
Try one non-numeric token and read the error.
Text becomes a number with astype.realWorld: CSV columns arrive as text; converting once at load time turns a column of strings into an array you can actually average.
mistakes: Calling `.mean()` on a string array and expecting a number.
Silently replacing unparseable values with 0 — that changes the mean.
Assuming `np.array` already parsed the numbers.
revision: astype(float) parses numeric text.
One bad token raises; validate which row failed.

steps: Divide an integer array by 2.
Print the result and its dtype.
Compare with `a // 2` for floor division.
Division always yields floats.realWorld: A ratio or percentage computed from integer counts must not silently stay an integer; true division is the default for exactly this reason.
mistakes: Expecting an integer result from `/`.
Using `//` when a fractional average is wanted.
Casting the result back to int before rounding.
revision: `/` always produces floats.
`//` is floor division and keeps integers.

steps: Cast `[0, 1, 2]` to bool.
Print the array and its dtype kind.
Sum the booleans to count the non-zero values.
Numbers become booleans by truthiness.realWorld: A presence column stored as 0/1 becomes a real mask with one cast, ready for filtering or counting.
mistakes: Expecting `False` only for exactly zero and `True` for negative values — negatives are True.
Casting NaN to bool and assuming it becomes False (it is True).
Using bool arrays for arithmetic when counts are wanted.
revision: Truthiness: zero is False, everything else True.
Bool sums count the True values.

steps: Build a boolean array and print it.
Call `.sum()` and print the count.
Compare with `len(a[a > threshold])`.
Count with a boolean array.realWorld: Dashboards count how many orders crossed a threshold by summing the mask — no loop, no branch.
mistakes: Using `sum()` on an object array where True is a string.
Forgetting the mask must match the array shape.
Counting with a Python loop when the mask already answers it.
revision: Booleans add as 1 and 0.
One mask serves counting, filtering and assignment.

dtype reports the element type.syntax: a.dtype  # one dtype for the whole array
steps: Create an int array and a float array.
Print both dtypes.
Mix an int and a float and print the promoted dtype.
dtype reports the element type.visual:
np.array([1, 2]).dtype   → int64
np.array([1.0]).dtype     → float64
int + float               → float64
dtype reports the element type.realWorld: A join silently turns an id column into float64 because one missing value introduced NaN; checking `.dtype` catches it before the ids print as `1.0`.
mistakes: Assuming each element can have its own dtype.
Ignoring the promotion that a single float literal causes.
Comparing dtype objects as strings instead of using `.kind`.
revision: One dtype per array.
Mixing types promotes to one that can hold both.

steps: Print an integer array.
Print a float array with the same values.
Point at the decimal point as the visual dtype cue.
A float array prints a decimal point.realWorld: In a notebook, the printed form is the fastest dtype check before a plot or a division looks wrong.
mistakes: Reading `[1. 2.]` as text rather than floats.
Assuming trailing dots are a formatting bug.
Trusting the print over `.dtype` in production code.
revision: A decimal point in the print means floats.
`.dtype` is the authoritative check.

steps: Print `itemsize` for int64 and int32.
Multiply by the element count to get `nbytes`.
Estimate the memory for ten million values.
Each dtype has a size in bytes.realWorld: Sizing a batch before loading it: 10 million int64 features need 80 MB before any copy, which decides whether the job fits on the worker.
mistakes: Confusing `itemsize` with `size`.
Forgetting that a copy doubles the footprint.
Assuming all integer dtypes are the same width.
revision: `itemsize` = bytes per element.
`nbytes` = itemsize × size.

steps: Compare an integer array with 1.
Print the result and its dtype.
Use the result to index the array.
A comparison produces booleans.realWorld: Filters, alerts and counts all start as a comparison; understanding that a mask is a real bool array explains why it can be stored and reused.
mistakes: Chaining comparisons with `and`/`or` instead of `&`/`|`.
Forgetting parentheses around each comparison.
Mutating the mask and wondering why the filter changed.
revision: Comparisons produce bool arrays.
Combine masks with `&`, `|`, `~`, each in parentheses.

steps: Cast `[1.9, -1.9, 2.5]` straight to int and print.
Round first, then cast, and print again.
Compare the two results value by value.
Casting a float to an integer truncates.realWorld: Converting a measured score to an integer grade: the direct cast gives 89.9 → 89, the rounded one gives 90.
mistakes: Casting first and rounding the integer afterwards (too late).
Assuming `np.round` rounds .5 up — it rounds to even.
Using int32 for values that can exceed its range.
revision: Round before casting.
np.round uses round-half-to-even.

steps: Ask `np.result_type` for int32 and float32.
Add a Python float to an int8 array and print the dtype.
Use `np.promote_types` for two dtype strings.
Type promotion with result_type.realWorld: Before a big allocation, `result_type` tells you whether the operation will quietly widen to float64 and double the memory.
mistakes: Assuming int32 + float32 stays float32.
Forgetting that Python scalars participate in promotion.
Using `result_type` on arrays instead of dtypes.
revision: Promotion picks a dtype that can hold both inputs.
`result_type` predicts it without running the operation.
